Assignment 05 / Sculpting for Design

Essence in Subtraction

A rose, an expression, a patterned pillar. Finding a form by taking material away.

Floral foam · Plaster · Carving

Carving introduced a different kind of decision-making. As Medha notes in her submission, a removed element cannot simply be added back. The work follows her experiments with floral foam and Plaster of Paris.

01

Something growing from a block

The foam exercise called for an abstract form. Medha began without a fixed design, but wanted the piece to suggest growth or blooming. As she carved, that idea became an abstract rose with vine-like forms spreading out from the bud.

She enjoyed the way her visualisation gradually took shape as more material was removed. The finished form holds a contrast between the curled, enclosed centre and the lower forms extending out around it.

02

An expression in the eyes

For the smaller plaster carving, Medha wanted to create a face. She drew on manga she had read as a child, particularly the way a close view of the eyes can communicate a full expression through eye angles and eyebrows.

The carving translates that idea into a compact three-dimensional object. Shallow cuts establish the features, while the different views reveal how those incisions sit on the curved plaster surface.

03

A lesson in timing

The pillar explores simple carved patterns. Here the material also introduced a practical difficulty: Medha waited too long after setting the plaster, and it became hard to carve.

She remained satisfied with the result. In her reflection, the depth created by subtraction gives the surface an effect she compares to whittled wood. The repeating marks make the cuts themselves part of the piece’s character.

04

Learning through removal

Across the three studies, subtraction produces different results: a curling organic form, a suggested expression, and repeated surface pattern. Foam allowed an enjoyable, gradual exploration, while the hardened plaster made timing and material resistance more apparent.

The assignment records both the finished objects and what the making process taught her. Each cut changes the available form, making the act of removing material central to the work.
